Bob Tillman has owned a coin-operated laundromat here in the Mission District
for 20 years. In 2013, he decided to tear it down and build an eight-story
75-unit apartment building. Since nobody lives above the laundry, the project
wouldn't displace any residents. It would also be in a popular area near multiple public transit stops, which
qualified it for a streamlined approval process under state law. And the site
had another major advantage for avoiding red tape. It was already zoned for housing.
If you can't build here, then you can't build anywhere.
But San Francisco developers are required to get explicit permission from city officials for any new construction.
So, in early 2014, Tillman began submitting paperwork to the planning department.
I went through an environmental review, application for conditional use permit,
a planning commission hearing, which turned into a second planning commission hearing.
The commission ordered a detailed historical review based on a claim that various community groups had offices on
the property in the 1970s and '80s. The resulting 137-page study concluded that
the laundry did not merit historic landmark status.
That study cost me $23,000 and delayed me another 4 months.
In late 2017, the planning commission was finally ready to vote on Tillman's
project, 3 and 1/2 years after he first applied to build. But that's when the real fight started.
